title: Given two arrays representing the preorder and inorder traversal of a binary tree with unique values, reconstruct and return the original tree.
shortTitle: Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

s1_definition.profdef: Reconstructing a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals exploits two facts: the first element of preorder is always the root, and locating that root in the inorder array splits it into the left subtree's values on one side and the right subtree's values on the other. You recurse on those splits, using a map from value to inorder index for constant-time root location and a moving preorder pointer.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has two records of the same org chart taken in two different reading orders. The preorder record always lists a manager before their teams, so the very first name is the top manager. The inorder record lists the left team, then the manager, then the right team, so once Rajesh finds that top manager's name in the inorder record, everyone to the left is the left team and everyone to the right is the right team. He repeats this for each team to rebuild the whole chart.
s1_definition.oneliner: Preorder gives the next root, inorder splits that root into left and right subtrees, and recursion rebuilds the whole tree.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reconstructing a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals exploits two facts: the first element of preorder is always the root, and locating that root in the inorder array splits it into the left subtree's values on one side and the right subtree's values on the other. You recurse on those splits, using a map from value to inorder index for constant-time root location and a moving preorder pointer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has two records of the same org chart taken in two different reading orders. The preorder record always lists a manager before their teams, so the very first name is the top manager. The inorder record lists the left team, then the manager, then the right team, so once Rajesh finds that top manager's name in the inorder record, everyone to the left is the left team and everyone to the right is the right team. He repeats this for each team to rebuild the whole chart.

**One line to remember:** Preorder gives the next root, inorder splits that root into left and right subtrees, and recursion rebuilds the whole tree.

sections.s2_technical:
Preorder visits node, then left, then right, so the preorder array lists roots before their subtrees, and reading preorder left to right hands you the roots in the exact order you need them. Inorder visits left, then node, then right, so the position of a root in inorder cleanly partitions the remaining values into the left subtree, everything before it, and the right subtree, everything after it.

You keep a pointer into the preorder array that only moves forward, giving the next root each time. For example: `int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];`.

You find that root's index in the inorder array in constant time using a precomputed map from value to index. For example: `int mid = inorderIndexMap.get(rootValue);`. Building the map once avoids a linear search per node.

You then recursively build the left subtree from the inorder range before the root, and the right subtree from the range after it. The order matters: because preorder is node-left-right, you must build the left subtree before the right so the preorder pointer consumes values in the correct order. For example: `node.left = build(inLeft, mid - 1); node.right = build(inmid + 1, inRight);`.

The base case is when the inorder range is empty, meaning no nodes remain in that branch. The time complexity is linear because each node is created once and the map makes root location constant time; without the map it would be quadratic. The space is linear for the map and recursion. A senior nuance is that this reconstruction requires unique values, because duplicates would make the root's position in inorder ambiguous; with duplicates you cannot uniquely rebuild the tree from these two traversals.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an org hierarchy was exported from a legacy system as two separate traversal logs, a preorder log and an inorder log, with the tree structure itself lost. Operations must rebuild the actual tree to migrate it into the new system. This is exactly how Construct Tree from Traversals works.

Problem 2 — The rebuild must be efficient over large hierarchies, so locating each root cannot be a repeated linear scan. This is exactly why we precompute a value-to-inorder-index map for constant-time root location.

The mini-project builds a `RoleNode` class, a `TreeBuilderService` that reconstructs the tree using a preorder pointer and an inorder index map with logging, and a runnable demo that rebuilds a hierarchy and prints a level-order check.

sections.s5_journey:
The input preorder is Manager, CreditOfficer, Clerk, Verifier, RiskHead and the inorder is Clerk, CreditOfficer, Verifier, Manager, RiskHead.

Step 1: The service builds the inorder index map: Clerk at zero, CreditOfficer at one, Verifier at two, Manager at three, RiskHead at four.

Step 2: The build starts with the full inorder range zero to four. The preorder pointer takes Manager as the root and advances. Manager is at inorder index three, so the left subtree spans inorder indices zero to two and the right subtree spans index four.

Step 3: It builds the left subtree over range zero to two. The preorder pointer takes CreditOfficer as the next root. CreditOfficer is at inorder index one, so its left subtree is range zero to zero and its right subtree is range two to two.

Step 4: It builds CreditOfficer's left over range zero to zero. The pointer takes Clerk. Clerk is at index zero, so both its sub-ranges are empty and Clerk is a leaf.

Step 5: It builds CreditOfficer's right over range two to two. The pointer takes Verifier. Verifier is at index two, both sub-ranges empty, so Verifier is a leaf.

Step 6: Back at the root, it builds Manager's right subtree over range four to four. The pointer takes RiskHead. RiskHead is at index four, both sub-ranges empty, so RiskHead is a leaf.

Step 7: The preorder pointer has consumed all five roles in order, and the rebuilt tree has Manager at the root with CreditOfficer and RiskHead as children, and Clerk and Verifier under CreditOfficer, exactly matching the original.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reconstructing a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals rests on two facts that fit together perfectly. Preorder visits node then left then right, so reading preorder from the front always hands me the next root in exactly the order I need. Inorder visits left then node then right, so the position of that root inside the inorder array splits the remaining values cleanly into the left subtree before it and the right subtree after it.

My implementation keeps a single forward-moving pointer into the preorder array to supply each root, and a precomputed map from value to inorder index so I can locate any root's split point in constant time. I recurse by passing down the current inorder range, creating a node from the next preorder value, looking up its split point, and building the left subtree over the range before it and the right subtree over the range after it. The order is critical: I must build the left subtree before the right, because preorder consumes node, then left, then right, and swapping them would hand the wrong values to each side.

Without the index map, locating each root would be a linear scan and the whole thing would be quadratic; with the map it is linear overall. I also point out that this reconstruction requires unique values, because a duplicate would make the root's position in inorder ambiguous and the tree could not be uniquely rebuilt from these two traversals.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to migrate an org hierarchy that a legacy system had exported only as two separate traversal logs, with the structure itself lost. The service rebuilt the actual tree from the preorder and inorder logs so it could be loaded into the new system, and the value-to-index map kept the rebuild fast even for large hierarchies.
